title: 324. Geometry, Spatial Thinking & Measurement: Constructing Perpendicular Bisectors
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the correct definition of the perpendicular bisector of a segment.
questions.question: Which statement correctly defines the perpendicular bisector of a segment?

options.label: A
options.text: A line that intersects a segment at its midpoint but is not necessarily perpendicular to the segment.

options.label: B
options.text: A line that is perpendicular to a segment at its midpoint.

questions.explanation: A perpendicular bisector of a segment is a line that passes through the midpoint of the segment and is perpendicular to the segment. Option A describes a line through the midpoint but does not require perpendicularity, so it is incomplete. Therefore, the correct definition is given by option B.
questions.hint: Recall that a perpendicular bisector must satisfy two conditions: passing through the midpoint and being perpendicular to the segment.

questions.concept: Equidistance Property of a Perpendicular Bisector
questions.learningObjective: Identify the equidistance property of points on a perpendicular bisector.
questions.question: Which statement is true for any point on the perpendicular bisector of segment \(AB\)?

options.label: A
options.text: The point is closer to one endpoint than to the other.

options.label: B
options.text: The point is equidistant from \(A\) and \(B\).

questions.explanation: A defining property of the perpendicular bisector is that every point on it is the same distance from both endpoints of the segment. Therefore, any point on the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\) is equidistant from \(A\) and \(B\). Option A contradicts this property.
questions.hint: Use the perpendicular bisector theorem, which relates points on the bisector to distances from the endpoints.

questions.concept: Compass-and-Straightedge Construction of a Perpendicular Bisector
questions.learningObjective: Identify the correct first step in constructing a perpendicular bisector.
questions.question: To construct the perpendicular bisector of segment \(AB\) using a compass and straightedge, which step is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Place the compass at \(A\) and at \(B\) with the same radius greater than half of \(AB\), and draw arcs that intersect above and below \(AB\).

options.label: B
options.text: Place the compass at the midpoint of \(AB\) only, and draw a circle with radius equal to \(AB\).

questions.explanation: The standard construction requires drawing arcs from both endpoints \(A\) and \(B\) using the same compass radius, which must be greater than half the length of \(AB\). These arcs intersect at two points, and the line through those points is the perpendicular bisector. Option B does not use both endpoints and does not produce the required construction.
questions.hint: Remember that the construction uses equal-radius arcs from both endpoints of the segment.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the midpoint of a segment from its endpoints.
questions.question: A segment has endpoints \(A(2,3)\) and \(B(8,7)\). What is the midpoint of \(AB\)?
questions.explanation: The midpoint formula gives the midpoint as \(\left(\frac{2+8}{2}, \frac{3+7}{2}\right)\). This simplifies to \(\left(\frac{10}{2}, \frac{10}{2}\right) = (5,5)\). Therefore, the midpoint of \(AB\) is \((5,5)\).
questions.hint: Add the corresponding coordinates of the endpoints and divide each sum by \(2\).

questions.learningObjective: Determine the slope of the perpendicular bisector of a segment.
questions.question: Segment \(AB\) has endpoints \(A(1,2)\) and \(B(5,6)\). What is the slope of the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\)?
questions.explanation: The slope of \(AB\) is \(\frac{6-2}{5-1} = \frac{4}{4} = 1\). A perpendicular line has a slope that is the negative reciprocal of \(1\), which is \(-1\). Therefore, the slope of the perpendicular bisector is \(-1\).
questions.hint: First find the slope of \(AB\), then take its negative reciprocal.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the equation of a perpendicular bisector from the midpoint and segment slope.
questions.question: A segment has midpoint \((2,3)\) and its slope is \(2\). Which equation represents the perpendicular bisector of the segment?
questions.explanation: The perpendicular bisector passes through the midpoint \((2,3)\) and has slope \(-\frac{1}{2}\), the negative reciprocal of \(2\). Using point-slope form gives \(y - 3 = -\frac{1}{2}(x - 2)\). Simplifying: \(y - 3 = -\frac{1}{2}x + 1\), so \(y = -\frac{1}{2}x + 4\). Therefore, the correct equation is option A.
questions.hint: Use the midpoint for the point and the negative reciprocal of the segment slope for the slope.

questions.concept: Reason for Compass Radius in Construction
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the compass radius must exceed half the segment length in the construction.
questions.question: In the compass-and-straightedge construction of a perpendicular bisector, why is the compass radius chosen to be greater than half the length of the segment?

options.label: A
options.text: So that the arcs drawn from the two endpoints intersect at two points.

options.label: B
options.text: So that the arcs meet the segment exactly at its midpoint.

questions.explanation: If the radius is greater than half the segment length, arcs drawn from both endpoints with the same radius will intersect at two distinct points. The line through these two intersection points is the perpendicular bisector. If the radius were too small, the arcs would not intersect; if exactly half, they would meet at only one point. Therefore, the correct reason is option A.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the arcs when the radius is larger than half the distance between the endpoints.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a point that lies on the perpendicular bisector of a given segment.
questions.question: Segment \(AB\) has endpoints \(A(0,0)\) and \(B(6,0)\). Which point lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\)?
questions.explanation: The midpoint of \(AB\) is \((3,0)\). Since \(AB\) is horizontal, its perpendicular bisector is the vertical line \(x = 3\). A point on this line must have \(x\)-coordinate \(3\). The point \((3,5)\) satisfies this condition, while \((5,3)\) does not. Therefore, \((3,5)\) lies on the perpendicular bisector.
questions.hint: Find the midpoint of \(AB\) and determine the line that is perpendicular to \(AB\) at that midpoint.

questions.concept: Converse of the Perpendicular Bisector Theorem
questions.learningObjective: Apply the converse of the perpendicular bisector theorem to a point equidistant from two endpoints.
questions.question: If a point \(P\) satisfies \(PA = PB\), what can be concluded about \(P\)?

options.label: A
options.text: \(P\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\).

questions.explanation: The converse of the perpendicular bisector theorem states that if a point is equidistant from the endpoints of a segment, then it lies on the perpendicular bisector of that segment. Since \(PA = PB\), point \(P\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\). Option B is not necessarily true because \(P\) could be above or below the segment.
questions.hint: Recall the converse of the perpendicular bisector theorem, which starts from equal distances to the endpoints.

questions.concept: Equation of a Perpendicular Bisector from Coordinates
questions.learningObjective: Determine the equation of a perpendicular bisector given the endpoints of a segment.
questions.question: Segment \(AB\) has endpoints \(A(-1,2)\) and \(B(5,8)\). Which equation represents the perpendicular bisector of \(AB\)?
questions.explanation: The midpoint of \(AB\) is \(\left(\frac{-1+5}{2}, \frac{2+8}{2}\right) = (2,5)\). The slope of \(AB\) is \(\frac{8-2}{5-(-1)} = \frac{6}{6} = 1\). The perpendicular slope is \(-1\). Using point-slope form with midpoint \((2,5)\): \(y - 5 = -1(x - 2)\). Simplifying gives \(y - 5 = -x + 2\), so \(y = -x + 7\). Therefore, the perpendicular bisector is \(y = -x + 7\).
questions.hint: Find the midpoint and the slope of \(AB\), then use the negative reciprocal slope with the midpoint.
